analysis.one_liner: Requires new cars to have auto-reversing power windows, better rear visibility, and anti-rollover brake features to protect children.
analysis.headline: The child car-safety bill drew 26 bipartisan cosponsors but never got a Senate vote, dying in the Commerce Committee when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Transportation to write safety rules for all new passenger vehicles: power windows that automatically reverse when they detect an obstruction, a standard for drivers to see people and objects behind the vehicle, and a requirement that the brake stay engaged so cars cannot roll away unexpectedly. It also would have created a public database of injuries and deaths in non-traffic, non-crash events (like backovers and children trapped in windows) and a public education program on those hazards [S2][S3]. Automakers would have had to add the equipment to new vehicles within a few years [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and young children, plus disabled people who are especially vulnerable to being backed over. The bill targeted the deaths and injuries that happen off the road — children backed over by vehicles, strangled by power windows, or hurt when cars roll away — events that today are not systematically counted anywhere [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires all new passenger vehicles to have power windows and panels that automatically reverse when they detect an obstruction, to stop children from being trapped, injured, or killed [S3].

Requires a rearward visibility performance standard so drivers can detect a person or object behind the vehicle, aimed at preventing backover deaths, especially of small children and disabled people [S2][S3].

Requires the service brake to be engaged in all key positions and while the key is out of the ignition, before the engine starts or the transmission engages, to prevent cars from rolling away accidentally [S3].

Directs the Transportation Secretary to build a public database of injuries and deaths in nontraffic, noncrash events — by make, model, and cause — and run a consumer education program on hazards like backovers, hot-car deaths, and power windows [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, which would have had to design and install the required safety equipment on all new vehicles within three years of final rules; those costs would flow partly into vehicle prices [S3].

drawbacks.text: The mandates apply to every new passenger vehicle regardless of size or price, so compliance costs would be spread across all buyers, including people shopping for the cheapest cars [S3].

Automatic-reversing window mechanisms and rear-visibility equipment can add complexity and cost to vehicles, and the bill left the details — including how fast the phase-in had to happen — up to the Secretary rather than fixing them in law [S3].
The database and education program add reporting and paperwork obligations for the Transportation Department and indirectly for anyone whose records feed the injury data [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety measures target a real, deadly, and poorly tracked category of harm — children and disabled people killed in driveway backovers, window entrapments, and rollaways — while the costs are the ordinary kind of vehicle-safety compliance costs that have historically been modest per car once rules are phased in. The main design criticism is that one-size mandates touch every vehicle and that key details were delegated to regulators rather than settled in the statute.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in November 2005 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it; it died there when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Hillary Clinton and Sen. John Sununu introduced the bill together on November 1, 2005, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee the same day [S1][S3][S5].
Twenty-six senators cosponsored the bill — 9 Republicans, 16 Democrats, and 1 Independent — giving it bipartisan support [S4].
No further action ever followed the referral: the committee never reported the bill, and the full Senate never debated or voted on it before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers were better off, because they avoided mandatory auto-reversing windows, rear-visibility equipment, and anti-rollaway brakes on all new vehicles for another two years, and the families the bill was named for got no new protections from this bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a bipartisan pair of introducers (a Democrat from New York and a Republican from New Hampshire) and 26 cosponsors split 9 Republican, 16 Democrat, and 1 Independent; opposition was not a party vote but a committee that simply never acted [S3][S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have forced every new passenger vehicle to carry auto-reversing power windows, rear-visibility equipment, and anti-rollaway brake features within three years of final rules [S3]. A bill like this stalled for two years saves manufacturers the retooling and per-vehicle cost of those systems, which is why the industry's interest in letting it sit runs against the families the rules would protect.
